edges.effect_quant: The strongest pooled randomized evidence shows that hibiscus lowers systolic blood pressure by roughly 6 to 8 mm Hg versus placebo in adults with mild-to-moderate hypertension. The evidence base is not women-only, but it is consistent enough to support a real antihypertensive signal in women as part of a broader adult population.
edges.population: adult women within mixed-sex cohorts of prehypertensive or mildly hypertensive adults consuming hibiscus preparations
edges.mechanism: Hibiscus appears to lower blood pressure through a combination of anthocyanin-rich antioxidant effects, mild natriuresis, and angiotensin-converting-enzyme inhibition. That mechanism fits the fact that the signal looks stronger in uncomplicated mild hypertension than in heavily medicated populations.
edges.summary: Hibiscus tea has enough randomized evidence behind it to be more than a folk remedy. Two meta-analyses and a placebo-controlled feeding trial point in the same direction: regular hibiscus intake lowers blood pressure modestly, although the supporting studies were not designed specifically for women alone.
edges.caveats: The underlying trials differ in dose, extract standardization, tea preparation, and comparator, so the exact effect size should not be overclaimed. This edge is about modest blood-pressure improvement, not cardiovascular-outcome reduction.

evidence.citation: AbdelmonemM et al 2022 J Cardiovasc Pharmacol
evidence.notes: Efficacy of Hibiscus sabdariffa on Reducing Blood Pressure in Patients With Mild-to-Moderate Hypertension: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Published Randomized Controlled Trials.
